## Systems Stress-Tests {#sec-boundary-1-10}

With the core architectural principles, physical archetypes, bedrock laws, and dual-brain silicon partitioning established, an engineer must be able to diagnose complex, borderline systems in the field. The following four systems stress-tests serve as capstone analytical exercises, challenging you to apply the scope test, physical limiting budgets, and proposal–permission contracts to real-world edge cases:

### Stress-Test 1: The Advisory Observer (Perception Without Actuation Authority) {.unnumbered}

*The scenario.* An automotive driver assistance module executes a 50-layer deep convolutional network to detect highway lane markings, sounding an auditory buzzer whenever the vehicle drifts across a boundary.

*The systems dilemma.* The system satisfies Criterion 1 (learned perception model) and Criterion 2 (vehicle motion continuously shifts camera viewpoints). However, it completely lacks Criterion 3 (delegated physical authority). Because its only output is an auditory chime, an algorithmic failure or inference stall cannot directly alter steering torque or vehicle momentum.

*The systems verdict: Advisory Decision Support.* The system operates entirely behind glass, relying on the human driver to provide physical closed-loop actuation.

### Stress-Test 2: The Deterministic Autopilot (Actuation Without Learned Models) {.unnumbered}

*The scenario.* An acrobatic quadrotor executes extreme trajectory tracking through turbulent outdoor wind gusts, calculating motor PWM commands at $1000\text{ Hz}$ on a bare-metal microcontroller [@maxwell1868governors].

*The systems dilemma.* The system satisfies Criterion 2 (rotor thrust directly accelerates physical mass) and Criterion 3 (microcontroller latches write directly to motor inverter registers without human intervention). However, it lacks Criterion 1 (learned model). The autopilot control law is derived from analytical Newton-Euler equations and linear state-space feedback whose stability margins are proven mathematically in closed form.

*The systems verdict: Classical Control Theory.* It requires hard real-time execution, but does not involve stochastic neural representations.

### Stress-Test 3: The Virtual Agent (Autonomy Without Physical Feedback) {.unnumbered}

*The scenario.* An automated high-frequency trading engine executes thousands of market transactions per second using deep transformer sequence models to predict price fluctuations.

*The systems dilemma.* The system satisfies Criterion 1 (deep learned predictive model) and Criterion 3 (automated execution of transactions without human approval). However, it lacks Criterion 2 (consequential physical feedback). Its outputs alter electronic memory buffers and order-book records, but do not interact with momentum, contact friction, or thermodynamic heat.

*The systems verdict: Digital Autonomous Systems.* If an algorithm diverges, market circuit breakers can freeze accounts, unwind transactions, and restore clean database states—privileges unavailable in the physical universe.

### Stress-Test 4: The Shared-Autonomy Reflex Gate (The Neuromuscular Latency Threshold) {.unnumbered}

*The scenario.* A robotic surgical scalpel applies learned haptic guidance forces to keep a surgeon's tool tip within a safe anatomical resection zone.

*The systems dilemma.* The system satisfies Criterion 1 (learned anatomical spatial models) and Criterion 2 (tool forces directly deform living tissue). Whether it satisfies Criterion 3 depends strictly on the actuator force rise time relative to human neuromuscular reflex latency ($150\text{--}250\text{ ms}$). If the haptic actuator can apply forces within that $200\text{ ms}$ window, the learned policy exercises transient, uncontested physical authority over tissue before the human surgeon can react.

*The systems verdict: Physical AI (Shared Autonomy).* The system requires a deterministic bare-metal safety filter to clip tool forces and prevent tissue damage during neural inference anomalies.

## Summary {#sec-boundary-1-11}

The causal boundary is the physical interface where digital information irreversibly converts into physical energy. It is not an abstract concept, but a physical line drawn at the memory-mapped registers of motor inverters, valve solenoids, and power stages.

Surviving this boundary requires organizing the machine into three distinct subsystems with separate operational responsibilities. The body consists of the linkages, transmissions, motor windings, and fluid conduits that move mass, exert contact force, or regulate a thermodynamic flow. The body obeys classical mechanics and electromagnetism rather than software instructions. The brain comprises the high-capacity learned models running on application processors. The brain provides semantic competence precisely because its weights are learned from data rather than hand-written, yet it remains unaccountable for the exact same reason. Between them sits the nervous system, the deterministic computing substrate that carries signals under strict deadlines dictated by the body. The nervous system executes low-level tracking loops, monitors sensor freshness, and evaluates physical safety invariants on isolated real-time silicon. Because it directly controls the gate drivers and timer peripherals, the nervous system is the only subsystem with the electrical authority to refuse an unsafe proposal and command a controlled stop.

Four bedrock laws govern every interaction across this tripartite structure. First, the law of physical causality and irreversibility establishes that physical actions are permanent; stored kinetic energy and dissipated heat cannot be rolled back with an exception handler. Second, the law of information freshness dictates that physical dynamics evolve continuously without waiting for neural inference. Dynamic stability and obstacle avoidance are bounded by worst-case latency percentiles ($P_{99}$) and sensory age, meaning that computational delay is always paid in physical displacement. Third, the law of proposal and permission privilege requires an absolute separation between cognitive intention and motor authority. High-capacity learned models operate strictly as untrusted proposal generators, while deterministic permission supervisors executing in zero-allocation static memory retain exclusive authority over actuator drive stages. Fourth, the law of governed change and defensible release demands that physical policies be qualified through cross-layer fault injection and formal safety cases. Because an acting machine alters its own operational data distribution, unmasked safety interventions corrupt training logs, and empirical demonstrations cannot substitute for verified safety envelopes.

The physical floor manifests differently across the three canonical machine classes, but each class hits an unyielding mechanical or electrical limit. In mobility systems, machines navigate continuous space under the constraints of momentum conservation ($p = mv$) and friction limits. For an autonomous rover traveling at $2.0\text{ m/s}$, an unbudgeted $250\text{ ms}$ inference stall adds $50\text{ cm}$ of unguided displacement before braking can begin, rapidly exhausting available stopping clearance. In contact manipulation, articulated linkages interact with stiff physical environments where contact forces scale steeply with minute positional errors. An overshoot of just $1.5\text{ mm}$ against a steel fixture generates massive instantaneous shock force, threatening to chip gear teeth in precision cycloidal drives. In cybernetic energy and process systems, learned policies govern continuous flows of current and fluid. A grid-tied power inverter operating on a $60\text{ Hz}$ utility network faces an electrical cycle of $16.6\text{ ms}$, where an unhandled scheduling delay creates alternating-current phase angle errors that drive destructive surge currents through substation transformers.

The physical limits governing these machines have been named conceptually, but naming a limit does not provide the quantitative physical budgets required to engineer an embodied system. An engineer cannot verify a safety case or configure a real-time permission supervisor using qualitative descriptions alone. Defending a machine against failure requires knowing the exact microsecond waterfall from photon arrival to motor current rise, the thermal capacitance that limits continuous stall torque, the mechanical contact impedance of the workpiece, and the memory bus contention that inflates neural inference tail latencies ($P_{99}$).

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Key Takeaways"}
- **The Causal Boundary is a Physical Address:** Informational abstraction ends at the memory-mapped registers of an actuator gate driver, where bits convert irreversibly into magnetic flux, kinetic momentum, and Joule heat.
- **The Tower of Babel Crisis:** Embodied AI fails when ML, Systems, Controls, and Safety operate in isolation; Physical AI synthesizes them into a unified systems discipline.
- **The Three Machine Archetypes:** Physical machines divide into Mass-Dominated (Class 1), Contact-Dominated (Class 2), and Flow-Dominated (Class 3) plants, each bound by a distinct mechanical or thermodynamic floor.
- **The Three-Pillar Scope Test:** A system requires Physical AI engineering only when it combines an unspecifiable learned model, consequential closed-loop physical feedback, and delegated actuator authority.
- **The Dual-Brain Architecture:** Untrusted neural policies running on application processors (MPUs) generate action proposals, while deterministic real-time microcontrollers (MCUs) evaluate physical invariants and retain exclusive authority to execute or veto commands.
:::

Chapter 2 transitions from conceptual boundaries to physical metrology on the hardware floor. By attaching measuring instruments directly to the compute substrate, the power electronics, and the mechanical linkages, we derive the governing equations and measurement disciplines for time, inertia, actuation, energy, and silicon. That quantitative accounting establishes the firm numerical budgets that every subsequent chapter must respect.

[^fn-trans-idempotency]: **For the Physical Engineer:** *Idempotency* in digital software means an operation can be executed multiple times without changing the final state (e.g., refreshing a webpage or retrying a database write). In physical systems, no operation is idempotent—every motor command consumes irreversible energy and alters the physical environment.

[^fn-hw-tim-pwm]: Power inverter timers enforce dead-time insertion ($50\text{--}500\text{ ns}$) to prevent shoot-through short circuits across DC buses. On ARM Cortex-M (`TIM1`/`TIM8`), capture/compare registers `TIMx_CCR` and preload register `TIMx_CCMR` buffer duty cycles until counter overflow to eliminate pulse glitches, mirrored in TI C2000 `ePWM` shadow registers.

[^fn-hw-serdes-bus]: Automotive SerDes links (TI FPD-Link III, ADI GMSL2/3) serialize multi-gigabit MIPI CSI-2 sensor streams over coaxial cables with sub-$15\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ transfer latency, hardware CRC-32 verification, and bidirectional backchannel `FSYNC` triggers that align multi-camera exposure start times within sub-microsecond jitter.

[^fn-math-contact-lcp]: Rigid contact mechanics obey Signorini-Coulomb complementarity ($0 \le \delta \perp F_N \ge 0$). Because ideal rigid impacts cause discontinuous acceleration spikes, real-time control stacks approximate compliance via spring-damper Kelvin-Voigt models or Linear Complementarity Problems (LCP) to prevent force loop divergence.

[^fn-inc-uber-tempe]: NTSB Highway Accident Report NTSB/HAR-19/03 (2019). The investigation established that semantic classification toggling repeatedly reset tracking histories and suppressed emergency braking for $1.2\text{ s}$, while factory autonomous emergency braking was disabled to prevent diagnostic bus conflicts with the prototype software stack.

[^fn-std-iso26262]: Safety-critical systems combine deterministic functional safety (ISO 26262 ASIL-D, IEC 61508 SIL-3) with autonomous system standards: ISO 21448 (SOTIF) governs perception hazards and out-of-distribution limits, while UL 4600 mandates goal-structured safety cases requiring guaranteed transitions to a Minimal Risk Condition (MRC) upon subsystem anomaly.

[^fn-hw-ptp-timestamps]: To counter $20\text{--}50\text{ ppm}$ thermal clock drift across sensors, physical AI networks utilize IEEE 802.1AS (gPTP) or IEEE 1588v2. Automotive Ethernet PHYs capture hardware timestamps at the MAC layer's Start-of-Frame Delimiter with $< 10\text{ ns}$ precision, ensuring sub-microsecond temporal alignment.

[^fn-hw-soc-mailbox]: In heterogeneous SoCs (e.g., TI Sitara AM64x, NXP i.MX8M), Linux MPUs and real-time Cortex-M/R MCUs exchange data across non-cached dual-port SRAM via OpenAMP/RPMsg mailboxes. Out-of-order MPU cores require explicit Data Memory Barriers (`DMB`) and cache flushes before asserting Inter-Processor Interrupts (`IPI`) to prevent torn memory reads.

[^fn-hw-mems-acoustic]: MEMS gyroscopes rely on silicon proof masses oscillating at $18\text{--}32\text{ kHz}$. Ultrasonic acoustic attacks tuned to these resonant modes induce structural resonance, saturating capacitive amplifiers and spoofing Coriolis accelerations. Physical AI mitigates acoustic spoofing through hermetic dampening, dual-proof-mass topologies, and MCU-level kinematic plausibility cross-checks.
